lines.text: Why do wet fingers wrinkle? Your arm stays smooth in the same bath.
lines.phonemes: wˌaɪ dˈuː wˈɛt fˈɪŋɡəz ɹˈɪŋkəl? jɔːɹ ˈɑːm stˈeɪz smˈuːð ɪnðə sˈeɪm bˈaθ.

lines.text: It looks like skin soaking up water and swelling, like a sponge. It's the story we grew up with, and it's wrong.
lines.phonemes: ɪt lˈʊks lˈaɪk skˈɪn sˈəʊkɪŋ ˌʌp wˈɔːtə and swˈɛlɪŋ, lˈaɪk ɐ spˈʌndʒ. ɪts ðə stˈɔːɹi wiː ɡɹˈuː ˈʌp wɪð, and ɪts ɹˈɒŋ.

lines.text: Almost a century ago, doctors noticed something odd: a finger whose nerve had been cut stayed perfectly smooth in the bath.
lines.phonemes: ˈɔːlməʊst ɐ sˈɛntʃəɹi ɐɡˈəʊ, dˈɒktəz nˈəʊtɪst sˈʌmθɪŋ ˈɒd: ɐ fˈɪŋɡə hˌuːz nˈɜːv hɐdbɪn kˈʌt stˈeɪd pˈɜːfɛktlˌɪ smˈuːð ɪnðə bˈaθ.

lines.text: So the wrinkles come from your nerves. In water, they narrow the tiny vessels under each fingertip, the pad shrinks a little, and the skin on top buckles.
lines.phonemes: sˌəʊ ðə ɹˈɪŋkəlz kˈʌm fɹɒm jɔː nˈɜːvz. ɪn wˈɔːtə, ðeɪ nˈaɹəʊ ðə tˈaɪni vˈɛsəlz ˌʌndəɹ ˈiːtʃ fˈɪŋɡətˌɪp, ðə pˈad ʃɹˈɪŋks ɐ lˈɪtəl, and ðə skˈɪn ˌɒn tˈɒp bˈʌkəlz.

lines.text: A wrinkle is a reflex, one doctors use to test a nerve. Why we have it is argued: one study found a wet grip, the next found none.
lines.phonemes: ɐ ɹˈɪŋkəl ɪz ɐ ɹˈiːflɛks, wˈɒn dˈɒktəz jˈuːs tə tˈɛst ɐ nˈɜːv. wˌaɪ wiː hav ɪt ɪz ˈɑːɡjuːd: wˈɒn stˈʌdi fˈaʊnd ɐ wˈɛt ɡɹˈɪp, ðə nˈɛkst fˈaʊnd nˈɒn.

lines.text: It only happens on the hairless skin of hands and feet, which also carry the thickest dead layer, nearly two sheets of paper.
lines.phonemes: ɪt ˈəʊnli hˈapənz ɒnðə hˈeələs skˈɪn ɒv hˈandz and fˈiːt, wˌɪtʃ ˈɔːlsəʊ kˈaɹi ðə θˈɪkɪst dˈɛd lˈeɪə, nˌiəli tˈuː ʃˈiːts ɒv pˈeɪpə.

lines.text: So your fingers don't wrinkle because they're soaked. They wrinkle because your nerves decide to.
lines.phonemes: sˌəʊ jɔː fˈɪŋɡəz dˈəʊnt ɹˈɪŋkəl bɪkˈɒz ðeɪə sˈəʊkt. ðeɪ ɹˈɪŋkəl bɪkˈɒz jɔː nˈɜːvz dɪsˈaɪd tuː.

lines.text: Next: is a tan really a shield for your skin?
lines.phonemes: nˈɛkst: ɪz ɐ tˈan ɹˈiəlɪ ɐ ʃˈiːld fɔː jɔː skˈɪn?
